findings.title: Undocumented SPI contract: raw recovery codes go to user storage as a JSON string, and label/created date are dropped
findings.body: For user-storage users, `createRecoveryCodesCredential` calls `updateCredential` with a `UserCredentialModel` whose value is a JSON array of the plaintext (unhashed) codes. The local path stores only hashed codes. The `credentialModel` built by the caller carries the creation time and user label, but neither reaches the storage provider. Nothing in the Javadoc or SPI documents that format. Provider authors must guess it, and the test stub only works because it hard-codes `JsonSerialization.readValue(..., List.class)`. The storage also has to implement one-time-use tracking on its own, because the form authenticator never marks a federated code as used. Document the expected contract (value format, plaintext codes, one-time use) in the Javadoc and the SPI docs, or pass the metadata through.

findings.title: Unguarded Optional.get() will 500 the login page when a federated provider is configured but returns no credential
findings.body: `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` now looks up federated credentials first and falls back to local ones. The bean still calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` and then `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` with no guard. The authenticator's `configuredFor` uses `isConfiguredFor`, which the provider answers separately from `getCredentials`. A storage provider that reports the type as configured but does not return a matching model from `getCredentials` therefore throws `NoSuchElementException` while rendering the recovery-code input form. The same happens if every code is already used. The feature now depends on providers implementing four methods consistently (`updateCredential`, `isValid`, `isConfiguredFor`, `getCredentials`). A misbehaving provider produces an unhandled exception instead of a clean error or a fall-back to reconfiguration.

findings.title: getCredentials dereferences a possibly-null MyUser and returns a recovery model without the stored ID
findings.body: `getMyUser(user)` returns null for a user not in the map, for example after `removeUser`. `getCredentials` then does `myUser.recoveryCodes` without a null check, so it throws an NPE. The other methods (`isConfiguredFor`, `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream`) do check for null. The recovery model returned is rebuilt with `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, which sets no ID. This discards the ID generated in `updateCredential`, so the credential Keycloak sees has a null ID. `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator` passes `getId()` to `removeStoredCredentialById` when all codes are used, and a null ID would break that. The user label is also read from a model that never sets it. The IOException handler logs without the exception. Add a null guard, and carry over the ID and metadata from the stored model.

findings.title: New test only covers the happy path; the stub does not model one-time codes or code progression
findings.body: `testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` sets up codes and logs in once with code #0. The stub's `isValid` accepts any stored code any number of times, and its `getCredentials` rebuilds the model from the original list. Every code therefore always looks unused and the form always asks for code 0. The test never exercises recovery codes being consumed, `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode` advancing, `allCodesUsed` triggering re-registration, or a wrong code being rejected. It also does not cover regenerating codes in user storage or the account REST/console view of the credential. Regressions in the user-storage path for these cases would go unnoticed.
